extractor.note: Partial pass over the Introduction, where the reduction is the commentary's explicit subject.

coverage_note: Covers the Introduction, 'The Phenomenological Reduction and the Subject's Double Life', through its Husserl half and the 'Heidegger' section (lines 23-88): the framing of the reduction, the Fink Sixth Cartesian Meditation material, and the comparison with Heidegger. The two Heidegger subsections that follow and the later chapters are not covered.

units.claim: The reduction is agreed across the current French debate to be a leading-back of philosophical thought to phenomena that the reduction itself first makes appear.
units.quote: Everyone treats the reduction as a leading-back (*Rückführung*) of philosophical thought to phenomena; but the phenomena in question are those whose appearing requires the reduction itself

units.claim: Bernet places the scission the reduction opens inside the phenomenological phenomenon itself rather than between phenomenological and ordinary phenomena.
units.quote: The scission the reduction introduces thus falls not between rational phenomenological phenomena and irrational ordinary ones but within the phenomenological phenomenon itself

units.claim: Husserl distinguishes the world-constituting subject, which the reduction exhibits, from the impartial spectator, which performs the reduction.
units.quote: the first is what the reduction gives to be seen, the second is the agent who performs it

units.primary_locator: La vie du sujet, p. 10; Fink, Sixth Cartesian Meditation
units.claim: Fink's text presents the ontological import of the Husserlian reduction as making the difference between the being of the world and the pre-being of transcendental consciousness appear.
units.quote: which is meant to make appear the difference between the "being" of the world and the "pre-being" (*Vor-Sein*) of transcendental consciousness

units.claim: The Sixth Meditation finds no motive within natural life capable of compelling the change of life the reduction requires.
units.quote: No difficulty met with in natural life, no desire for clarification, no will to do scientific work has the power to extract a human being from immersion in the natural life accomplished within the world.

units.claim: The passage from the natural to the phenomenological phenomenon is not a reflective doubling of consciousness but a scission, and neither the subject-object nor the higher-order-consciousness model of reflection applies.
units.quote: It neither sets the constituting subject before the gaze by separating it from the constituted object, nor makes constituting consciousness the object of a second constituting consciousness.

units.claim: What the spectator first makes appear is the ontological difference between constituting consciousness and constituted world, so the reduction's aim is ontological.
units.quote: What appears for the first time thanks to the spectator is the ontological difference between constituting consciousness and constituted world

units.claim: The split of the transcendental subject follows directly from the reduction: in the universal epoché the spectator produces itself by separating from constituting consciousness.
units.quote: The split (*Spaltung*) of the transcendental subject follows directly from the reduction: in the universal epoché the phenomenological spectator produces itself, separating itself from constituting consciousness in order to make the latter appear as its counterpart.

units.claim: The spectator, unlike constituting consciousness, has no anonymous pre-reductive existence in natural life.
units.quote: There is, by contrast, no phenomenological spectator that would be ignorant of itself while working anonymously in natural life — the spectator does not exist before the reduction.

units.claim: Husserl corrects Fink's account of the spectator's worldlessness by redescribing its disinterest as a different interest, in the world's origin in transcendental consciousness.
units.quote: Husserl's correction is the more accurate formulation: the spectator is interested in the origin of the world in transcendental consciousness, rather than uninterested in the world.

units.primary_locator: La vie du sujet, pp. 18-19; Heidegger 1927 course
units.claim: Heidegger keeps the reduction as a fundamental piece of phenomenological method while redirecting it from transcendental consciousness to the understanding of the being of a being.
units.quote: For Heidegger, it leads the gaze back from any grasp whatever of a being to the understanding of the being of that being, projected upon the mode of its unconcealment (*Unverborgenheit*).

units.claim: Anxiety performs in Heidegger what the reduction performs in Husserl and Fink, bringing Dasein before a new self and before the phenomenon of its own being.
units.quote: Like the reduction in Husserl and Fink, anxiety brings it about that Dasein, finding itself face to face and alone with itself, encounters for the first time not only a new self but the phenomenon of its own being.
